To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the duration of the euthermic interval during hibernation is dependent on body mass; (2) this relationship is similar to the relationship between mass and euthermic metabolic rate; (3) the duration of torpor is inversely related to body mass, and (4) the duration of euthemic intervals is much more important in determining the total amount of energy used to maintain high body temperatures during hibernation than is the number of arousals.

the durations of the intervals during hibernation are dependent on body mass, that this relationship supports the theory that the timing of changes of body temperature is controlled by some aspect of metabolism, and that small species remain torpid for longer periods and at lower temperatures than large species.
the durations of the euthermic and torpid intervals are both dependent on body mass in a manner consistent with the theory of metabolic regulation of the timing of body-temperature changes.
